title: Tokens: how a model reads
subtitle: Byte-pair encoding, merge by merge, with TinyGPT's real 256-token vocab

segments.text: Models can't read letters. They only eat numbers. So how does a word like Wednesday get in?
segments.scene: The word 'wednesday' in big letters above a box labelled 'the model — only eats numbers', with an arrow and '[ ?, ?, ? ]' between them.

objects.label: the word "wednesday"
TinyGPT only accepts integer token ids (0–255)

segments.text: The simplest trick is one number per character. Our model starts with 35 base symbols. 26 letters, space, newline, six punctuation marks, and an unknown token.
segments.scene: A grid of the 35 base tokens with their ids: <unk> (0), newline (1), space (2), a–z (3–28), and . , ? ! : ' (29–34).

token 1: newline
token 2: space

segments.text: Byte-pair encoding fixes this. First, chop the training text into words, each keeping its leading space. Merges never cross from one word into the next.
segments.scene: The corpus snippet 'tom has a blue boat. tom gives' is split into word pieces (tom · ␣has · ␣a · ␣blue · ␣boat · . · ␣tom · ␣gives), with yellow separators: merges never cross a word boundary.

segments.text: Then count every pair of neighbors inside those words, across the first 400 thousand characters. The winner is space t, 13,558 times. Merge it into a brand new token, and repeat.

title: Embeddings: words as directions
subtitle: The lookup table that turns token ids into 64 numbers, and the meaning hiding in them

segments.text: To this model, red is just token 157. A row number. So how does a number come to mean anything?
segments.scene: A big token chip '␣red' with its id 157 underneath and the question 'what does 157 mean?'.

objects.label: token " red" has id 157 in the 256-token vocabulary

segments.text: The very first step is a lookup table. 256 rows, one per token, 64 numbers in each row. Token 157 just grabs row 157. That row is its embedding.
segments.scene: The real 256×64 embedding table as a heatmap (orange positive, blue negative). Row 157 is outlined and slides out as a strip of 64 cells; its first values are -0.17, -0.14, -0.18, +0.07 … -0.19.

objects.label: token " red" has id 157 in the 256-token vocabulary
the real token-embedding table: 256 rows × 64 columns = 16,384 learned numbers
embedding of " red" (row 157): 64 numbers from -0.28 to +0.28, length 1.18

segments.text: All 16,384 numbers started as random noise. And the same table is reused at the very end, to score every possible next token. So training pulls tokens that fit the same slots toward similar rows.
segments.scene: Same view; captions: 'started random → shaped by training' and 'reused at the end to score every next token (weight tying)'. The table holds 16,384 of the model's 170,560 parameters.

objects.label: token " red" has id 157 in the 256-token vocabulary

segments.text: No single number means red. What matters is the direction the whole row points. We compare directions with cosine similarity: one means same way, zero means unrelated.
segments.scene: Toy 2-D picture: arrows for ' red' and ' purple' point almost the same way, ' tom' points elsewhere. Text: cosine similarity = how aligned two arrows are (+1 same way, 0 unrelated, −1 opposite).

objects.label: toy 2-D illustration of embedding directions (not real values)
cosine similarity: +1 same direction, 0 unrelated, −1 opposite

segments.text: Every token turns its vector into three new ones. A query that asks, what am I looking for. A key that says, here's what I've got. And a value, the info it hands over if it gets picked.

subtitle: The chain rule on a toy graph, then TinyGPT's real gradients for one prediction

segments.text: TinyGPT guessed red at 87 percent. Which of its 170,560 weights deserve the blame, and how much? Backprop answers for all of them, in one sweep backwards.
segments.scene: The end of the probe prompt '… tom has the' → ' red' at 87.1%, loss 0.138; below, a grid of dots standing for the model's 170,560 weights with the question 'which ones are to blame?'.

objects.label: TinyGPT predicts " red" with p = 0.8707
cross-entropy loss = −ln(0.8707) = 0.1385
TinyGPT has 170,560 trainable weights (dots are a stand-in)

segments.text: A toy version first. Forward: two times three is six, plus one is seven. That misses the target five by two. Squared, the loss is four.
segments.scene: Toy computational graph (labelled toy): x = 2 and w = 3 feed a × node giving a = 6; a and b = 1 feed a + node giving z = 7; (z − t)² with target t = 5 gives loss L = 4. Forward values in teal.

toy input w = 3
toy input b = 1
multiply node: a = w × x
add node: z = a + b
squared error node: L = (z − t)², target t = 5
forward value a = w·x = 6
forward value z = a + b = 7
toy loss L = (7 − 5)² = 4

segments.text: Now backwards. The slope at z is twice the miss: four. A plus node passes blame straight through: a and b get four. A times node scales it by the other input: w gets eight, x gets twelve.
segments.scene: Backward pass on the toy graph, arrows reversed, gradients in orange flowing right-to-left: ∂L/∂z = 2(z − 5) = 4; the + node copies it: ∂L/∂a = 4, ∂L/∂b = 4; the × node multiplies by the other input: ∂L/∂w = 4 × 2 = 8, ∂L/∂x = 4 × 3 = 12.

segments.text: Brute-force check: nudge w by a hair, and the loss moves eight times as much. Each node just multiplies the blame from above by its own local slope.

segments.text: Now the real thing. Each output logit's blame is its probability, minus one for the right answer. Red: minus 0.13, push up. White and purple: plus, push down.
segments.scene: Real gradient of the loss w.r.t. TinyGPT's output logits on the probe prompt (target ' red'): ∂loss/∂logit = p − onehot. ' red' -0.129 (teal, push up), ' white' +0.059, ' purple' +0.051, ' black' +0.0028, ' ava' +0.0015 (orange, push down); the other 251 are each between 0 and +0.0011.

segments.text: Take that step on every weight at once, and it overshoots: red falls to 51 percent. TinyGPT's training clips gradients longer than one, and this one is 7.95. Clipped, red rises to 87.5.

segments.text: And real training averages blame over 4,096 predictions per batch, uses 0.003 only as a cosine schedule's peak, and lets AdamW set each weight's step.
segments.scene: Real training differs from the toy step: averages over 4,096 predictions per batch, clips the gradient only when its length exceeds 1, uses lr 0.003 as the peak of a warmup + cosine schedule, and AdamW adapts each weight's step size.

segments.text: Why does backward cost about twice forward? Each forward matrix multiply needs two going back: blame for its inputs, and for its weights. So a training step is roughly three forward passes.
segments.scene: Matrix diagram: forward Y = X·W (one multiply); backward dX = dY·Wᵀ (blame for inputs) and dW = Xᵀ·dY (blame for weights): two multiplies. Tally: forward ≈ 1, backward ≈ 2, training step ≈ 3 units (approximate). Note: activations must be stored for the backward pass.

backward: dX = dY·Wᵀ passes the gradient to the layer's input
backward: dW = Xᵀ·dY is the gradient for the weights
rule of thumb: backward ≈ 2× forward FLOPs, so a training step ≈ 3× a forward pass (approximate; depends on implementation)
backprop needs the forward activations, so training uses much more memory than inference

segments.text: Forward, backward, nudge. In PyTorch, loss dot backward does the middle step for you. Go watch the gradients flow.

title: Optimizers: learning rate, momentum & Adam
subtitle: Why the learning rate is the knob that matters most, and why AdamW is the default (real sweeps)

segments.text: Same model, same data, same 1,000 steps. Only one number changed: the learning rate. And it decides everything.
segments.scene: Real validation-loss curves of TinyGPT trained 1000 steps with AdamW at 7 learning rates (1e-4 … 0.1): lr 1e-4 → 1.74, lr 3e-4 → 0.81, lr 1e-3 → 0.66, lr 3e-3 → 0.55, lr 0.01 → 0.55, lr 0.03 → 1.13, lr 0.1 → 3.72.

segments.text: Picture the loss as a landscape and the weights as a ball. The gradient is the slope under the ball. Step downhill by the learning rate times the slope. Repeat.
segments.scene: Toy 1-D loss landscape (illustration) with a yellow ball, an orange tangent showing the slope, and the update rule w ← w − lr × slope; the ball takes 8 steps downhill.

objects.label: toy loss landscape (illustration, one weight)
gradient descent update: w ← w − lr × slope

segments.text: Too small: you crawl. Just right: you settle in a few steps. Too big: every step overshoots, bouncing higher and higher.
segments.scene: Three toy bowls (illustration): too small (creeps), just right (settles), too big (overshoots, bouncing out of the valley).

objects.label: toy illustration: learning rate too small
toy illustration: learning rate just right
toy illustration: learning rate too big

segments.text: The real runs agree. Learning rate one e minus four is still crawling at 1.74. three e minus three reaches 0.55. At 0.1, it thrashes around and ends at 3.72.
segments.scene: Real AdamW validation curves: lr 1e-4 (too small) ends at 1.74, lr 3e-3 (best) ends at 0.55, lr 0.1 (too big) ends at 3.72.

real AdamW run, lr 3e-3: final val 0.55, best 0.546

segments.text: Loss landscapes often have long, narrow valleys. Plain gradient descent zigzags across the walls and creeps along the floor. Momentum adds up past gradients: the back-and-forth parts cancel, and the steady downhill part builds speed.
segments.scene: Toy 2-D elongated valley (illustration, contour ellipses), same learning rate 0.19 for both. Top: plain gradient descent zigzags for all 30 steps and ends 1.41 from the minimum; bottom: with momentum (β=0.5, v = 0.5·v + gradient) the zigzag dies out within ~8 steps and it ends 0.32 from the minimum.

segments.text: On the real model, the best plain SGD ends at 0.74. With momentum, 0.57, at a lower learning rate, since momentum sums gradients.
segments.scene: Real runs, best learning rate of each: SGD (lr 1) → 0.74, SGD + momentum 0.9 (lr 0.3) → 0.57.

segments.text: Here's the catch. At step zero, typical gradient sizes differ 274 times between weight tensors. One learning rate can't suit them all.
segments.scene: Real per-weight gradient size (RMS of the gradient) for 8 of TinyGPT's tensors at initialisation, log scale: from 7.1e-05 (blocks.0.ln1.weight) to 1.9e-02 (blocks.0.attn_out.bias), a 274× spread.

segments.text: Adam keeps two running averages for every weight: the gradient, which is momentum, and the gradient squared. Dividing one by the square root of the other gives each weight its own step size.
segments.scene: Adam's update: step = lr × avg(gradient) / √avg(gradient²). Top term = momentum (smoothed direction); bottom = each weight's own typical gradient size, so each weight moves at most about lr per step. PyTorch defaults β1 0.9, β2 0.999, + ε.

objects.label: Adam: step = lr × avg(g) / sqrt(avg(g²)) (+ small ε), per weight
Adam normalises step sizes per weight: at most about lr when the gradient sign is consistent, smaller when it is noisy
Adam hyper-parameters: beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999, epsilon 1e-8, with bias correction for the first steps

segments.text: AdamW adds weight decay, a small shrink of every weight each step, applied directly to the weights. In this one sweep its good range spans 10 times; momentum SGD's, 3; plain SGD never got close. That forgiveness is a big reason it's the usual default.

segments.text: Our real recipe also uses a schedule: warm up for 100 steps while Adam's averages are still noisy, then decay along a cosine so the model settles. The sweep kept the rate constant on purpose.
segments.scene: Real learning-rate schedule of the shipped TinyGPT recipe (train/train.py): linear warm-up over 100 steps to 0.003, then cosine decay to 0 at step 3000; plus gradient clipping at norm 1.0. The sweep in this video used a constant rate instead.

segments.text: Why? Training sends a gradient backward through every layer. Without the plus, each layer multiplies it by its own slope. In a deep plain stack that's about times 0.2 per layer, and twenty-four of those leave almost nothing.
segments.scene: Backward pass as a chain of ×0.19 pills (the real average per-layer shrink of the gradient in a 24-layer no-residual TinyGPT at init); 0.19^24 = 4.0e-18.

objects.label: each layer multiplies the backward gradient by ~0.19 (real average, 24-layer probe)

segments.text: Measured in a fresh 24-layer model: without residuals, the gradient reaching the first layer is 10 to the 17 times smaller than at the top. Forward, the signal keeps its size, but every position ends up holding the same vector. With residuals, the gradient is nearly flat.
segments.scene: Real measurement, a separate 24-layer TinyGPT at initialisation: RMS of the gradient reaching each layer (log scale). Without residuals (pink) it falls from 4.9e-04 at the top to 2.0e-21 at the input (×10^-17); with residuals (teal) it stays ≈ 5.5e-05–4.3e-05. Side note: without residuals the forward signal RMS stays 0.04–0.05, but positions become identical (spread 1.4e-07).

objects.label: real: gradient RMS without residuals, 4.92e-04 at the top layer → 1.98e-21 at the embeddings
without residuals the forward signal RMS stays 0.045–0.054 (LayerNorm rescales each block's input) but positions collapse: spread 1.4e-07 of the RMS at layer 24
real: gradient RMS with residuals, 4.33e-05 → 5.51e-05: nearly flat

segments.text: Our 3-layer model isn't that deep: its gradient shrinks only about 130 times. So how stuck it gets depends on the starting weights. With the standard small init, it stalls. Start the blocks larger, and the same plain stack does learn. Residuals make depth easy to train, whatever the init.

segments.text: As blocks keep adding edits, the stream itself grows. LayerNorm doesn't shrink it. It hands each block a rescaled copy: subtract the mean, divide by the spread, per token, then a learned gain and bias. Every block reads inputs of a sane size.

segments.text: Hypothesis: TinyGPT doesn't need its position embeddings. Attention by itself ignores word order, but the causal mask leaks some: each token sees a different number of tokens before it. So maybe it can work out positions on its own.
segments.scene: TinyGPT's input = token embedding + position embedding, with the position embedding crossed out: 'what if TinyGPT had no position embeddings?'. A 6×6 causal mask: token k sees k tokens, so some order information leaks in.

objects.label: token embedding: one learned vector per token (256 × 64)
position embedding: one learned vector per position (64 × 64 = 4,096 weights)
hypothesis: TinyGPT does not need learned position embeddings
causal mask: each position attends only to itself and earlier positions
the causal mask gives the model an implicit signal about position

segments.text: The smallest test: short runs of 600 steps, a few minutes at most on two CPU threads. Same code, same data, same batches, same seed. The baseline is unchanged TinyGPT; the only difference is one line.
segments.scene: Experiment setup (real): both runs use 600 steps, batch 64×64, AdamW lr 0.003, cosine schedule, seed 0, identical batches, CPU with 2 threads (30–235 s per run). Baseline: x = tok(idx) + pos(t). Variant: x = tok(idx).

objects.label: held fixed: 600 steps, batch 64×64, AdamW lr 3e-3 cosine, seed 0, same batches, same code
baseline: unchanged TinyGPT (170,560 params)
variant: position embedding removed (166,464 params used)

segments.text: Then compare, on held-out text, measured on the exact same batches. Baseline: 0.65. No positions: 0.68. Removing them hurt, by about 0.03.
segments.scene: Real validation-loss curves from step 200 to 600 (y axis zoomed to 0.62–0.92): baseline (blue) ends at 0.6524, no-positions (pink) ends at 0.6837; gap +0.0313. Evaluated on the same 24 held-out batches (98,304 tokens).

no-positions val loss: 0.896 at step 200 → 0.684 at step 600

segments.text: But one seed could be luck. So we ran two more seeds per arm, each with its own initial weights and batch order. Both numbers move, yet every seed agrees: no positions is worse, by 0.03 to 0.04. That gap beats the seed-to-seed spread.

segments.text: Three classic traps. Different compute: compare against the released model, trained five times longer, and the gap looks 7 times bigger than it is. Unfair tuning: the learning rate was picked for the baseline, not the variant. And leakage: 55 percent of held-out lines, 39 percent of the text, also appear in training.
segments.scene: Three trap cards. Different compute: comparing the 600-step no-positions run (0.684) to the released 3,000-step model (0.452, same eval batches) suggests a 0.232 gap, 7.4× the real 0.031. Unfair tuning: lr 0.003 was chosen for the baseline. Data leakage: 1,642 of 3,001 held-out lines (54.7%) appear verbatim in the training split: all 1,579 short templated lines (Q&A, counting, pets, days, facts) but only 8 of 526 trade stories; 38.5% of held-out characters.

segments.text: So at 600 steps, positions win. Now scale it up. The app's full 3,000-step ablation finds the gap all but closes: 0.450 versus 0.451. And papers report causal models can learn position without embeddings. Scaling is where ideas live or die. Your turn: pick a hypothesis.

title: The frontier: a map for model inventors
subtitle: RoPE, efficient attention, state-space models, GQA, MoE, distillation, retrieval, diffusion LMs, test-time compute, better training

segments.text: Want to invent a new kind of model? Here's a map of where people are pushing. Each idea changes one part of the engine TinyGPT runs on.
segments.scene: A map: TinyGPT's parts in the centre (tokens & positions, attention, MLP, next-token loss, generation loop) with ten research directions around it, grouped into clusters: long sequences & fast inference (RoPE, efficient attention, state-space/Mamba, grouped-query attention), more model per FLOP (mixture of experts, distillation), knowledge outside the weights (retrieval), new ways to generate (diffusion LMs, test-time compute), how it learns (better training). Dashed lines show which part each idea changes.

objects.label: TinyGPT component: tokens & positions
TinyGPT component: attention
TinyGPT component: MLP
TinyGPT component: next-token loss
TinyGPT component: generation loop
Positions & long context (RoPE): rotate each query and key by angles set by its position, so position enters the score as relative distance (replaces the position table)
Linear / efficient attention: approximate or restrict attention (kernel tricks, sparse or sliding windows) so cost grows ~linearly (changes attention)

State-space models (Mamba): a recurrence carries a fixed-size state along the sequence, yet still trains in parallel; Mamba makes its updates depend on the input (replaces attention (Mamba: the whole block))
Grouped-query attention: several query heads share one key/value head, so far less has to be cached per token (changes attention and the KV cache)
Mixture of experts: many expert MLPs; a learned router sends each token to a few: more parameters, not proportionally more compute (replaces the MLP)
Distillation & small models: train a small student on a big teacher's outputs: its full probabilities, or text it generated (changes the training target)
Retrieval-augmented models: look up relevant documents in an external store and put them into the context (adds to the input (what it reads))
Diffusion language models: start from a fully masked sequence and refine every position over a number of steps (replaces the left-to-right generation loop)
Test-time compute & reasoning: spend more compute per question: write out steps, or sample several answers and vote (changes how the generation loop is used)
Better training: the optimizer, the data and its order, the objective, RL after pretraining, the number format (changes how it learns, not what it is)

segments.text: State-space models like Mamba replace attention with a recurrence that carries a fixed-size state, so cost grows linearly with length. Open question: how much exact detail that state can hold.

segments.text: Grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key and value head. That shrinks the KV cache and speeds up generation, usually with little quality loss.
